issues.legal_issue: Knowingly attesting an affidavit as sworn and signed in the advocate’s presence when the deponent did not appear or sign before the advocate, thereby facilitating fraud, constitutes professional misconduct.
material_facts: The advocate attested an affidavit that purported to have been sworn and signed by the complainant in the advocate’s presence, although the complainant did not appear before him or sign the affidavit before him.
The advocate knew the complainant, and the evidence did not support the advocate’s explanation that the complainant had appeared and acknowledged the signature.
The affidavit was used to obtain an income-tax clearance certificate and facilitate registration of a disputed sale deed.
The advocate also falsely stated during the disciplinary inquiry that the complainant had appeared and acknowledged his signature.
The advocate was not authorised to attest an affidavit for a non-judicial purpose without the required State authorisation.
issues.conclusion: The advocate was guilty of gross professional misconduct.
issues.legal_principle: An affidavit is a sworn or affirmed statement, and its attestation signifies that the authorised officer administered the oath or received the affirmation and that the deponent signed in the officer’s presence. Section 3 of the Oaths Act, 1969, Rule 40 and Form No. 14 of the Civil Rules of Practice required those acts to be properly performed; Rule 34 authorised advocates to administer oaths for affidavits to be used in judicial proceedings, while a non-judicial affidavit required State authorisation. Part VI, Chapter II of the Bar Council of India Rules, 1975 requires advocates to maintain proper professional conduct and etiquette. The Court also relied on Krishan Chander Nayar v. The Chairman, Central Tractor Organisation for the responsibility attached to statements in affidavits, and Bar Council of Maharashtra v. M. V. Dabholkar for the public responsibilities inherent in the legal profession.

rule.if: advocate_disciplinary_proceeding and knowingly_false_attestation and affidavit_used_to_facilitate_fraud and false_account_to_disciplinary_body

predicates.advocate_disciplinary_proceeding: A proceeding concerns whether an advocate’s conduct amounts to professional misconduct.
predicates.knowingly_false_attestation: An advocate attests an affidavit as sworn and signed in the advocate’s presence while knowing that the deponent did not appear and sign before the advocate.
predicates.affidavit_used_to_facilitate_fraud: The falsely attested affidavit is used to obtain an official benefit or otherwise facilitate a fraud.
predicates.false_account_to_disciplinary_body: The advocate gives a disciplinary body an account of the attestation that the advocate knows to be false.
predicates.advocate_guilty_of_gross_professional_mi: The advocate’s conduct amounts to gross professional misconduct.

issues.definition: When an advocate in a disciplinary proceeding knowingly falsely attests an affidavit used to facilitate fraud and gives the disciplinary body a knowingly false account, the advocate is guilty of gross professional misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court’s appellate jurisdiction over a disciplinary decision includes authority, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, to vary the disciplinary committee’s finding as well as its punishment.
material_facts: The advocate appealed to the Supreme Court from a decision of the Bar Council of India’s Disciplinary Committee.
The Supreme Court issued notice that the punishment might be enhanced and heard the advocate before varying the disciplinary outcome.
The appellate committee had deleted findings that the Supreme Court considered supported by the record.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court had jurisdiction to vary the appellate committee’s finding and punishment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 38 of the Advocates Act, 1961, as amended by Act 60 of 1973, empowers the Supreme Court in an appeal from a decision of the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India to pass such order as it deems fit, including an order varying the punishment. That jurisdiction includes varying the committee’s finding, provided the affected person receives notice and an opportunity to be heard.

predicates.appeal_from_advocate_disciplinary_decisi: An appeal is brought to the Supreme Court from a disciplinary decision concerning an advocate.
predicates.notice_of_possible_adverse_change: The Supreme Court gives notice that it may make a change adverse to the advocate.
predicates.opportunity_to_be_heard: The advocate is given an opportunity to be heard before the Supreme Court makes that change.
predicates.supreme_court_may_vary_disciplinary_find: The Supreme Court may vary the disciplinary finding or punishment.

issues.definition: In an appeal from an advocate’s disciplinary decision, notice of a possible adverse change and an opportunity to be heard permit the Supreme Court to vary the finding or punishment.

issues.legal_issue: A reprimand is inadequate for grave professional misconduct involving knowing participation in forgery and the facilitation of fraud, and the punishment must be proportionate to the misconduct.
material_facts: The advocate knowingly attested a forged affidavit, facilitating the obtaining of an official certificate and the registration of a disputed sale deed.
The disciplinary committees had imposed and upheld only a reprimand despite finding misconduct.
The Supreme Court considered the misconduct grave and found the reprimand inadequate.
issues.conclusion: The reprimand was replaced with suspension from practice for five years.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35(3) of the Advocates Act, 1961 provides for reprimand, suspension from practice, or removal from the State roll. The punishment must be commensurate with the gravity of the misconduct. The Court relied on P. J. Ratnam v. D. K. Kanikaram, Bar Council of Maharashtra v. M. V. Dabholkar, and V. C. Rangadurai v. D. Gopalan in considering appropriate professional discipline.

predicates.advocate_disciplinary_appeal: An appeal concerns the punishment imposed for an advocate’s professional misconduct.
predicates.grave_professional_misconduct: The advocate’s misconduct is grave, including knowing participation in forgery or facilitation of fraud.
predicates.existing_reprimand_inadequate: The punishment imposed is only a reprimand and is inadequate in light of the gravity of the misconduct.
predicates.advocate_suspended_from_practice: The advocate is suspended from practice.

issues.definition: When an advocate’s disciplinary appeal concerns grave professional misconduct and the existing reprimand is inadequate, the advocate is suspended from practice.
